catalog_quote: [§5.4.2.1] The maximal extension of a LJG word is trisyllabic CV.CV.CCVC, as in /pə.la.kkǎy/ 'eagle'. In a trisyllable, C is obligatory in the onset of the antepenult, penult and ultima but optional in the coda of the ultima. Thus, the minimal form of a LJG trisyllable is CV.CV.CV, as in /kǝ.lu.lu/ 'rat'. The maximal extension of a LJG disyllable is CV.CCVC, as in /ma.ttǎh/ 'eye' and its minimal form is CV.V, as in /di.o/ 'far' or V.CV, as in /e.ko/ 'tail'. The minimal form of a LJG monosyllable is CV, as in /ma/ 'forest', or VC, as in / iɁ/ 'yes'. The language does not possess lexemes that contain four or more syllables. Like the other Berawan languages, LJG has Jnal [sic, text-layer for 'final'; fi-ligature lost] syllable stress. ... new_statements.quote: The maximal extension of a LJG word is trisyllabic CV.CV.CCVC, as in /pə.la.kkǎy/ 'eagle'. [...] The language does not possess lexemes that contain four or more syllables. Like the other Berawan languages, LJG has final syllable stress. [§5.4.2.1, p.77] — [§6.5.1, p.193:] Since all Berawan languages possess ultimate syllable stress, PBn etyma are reconstructed with ultimate syllable stress. — [§6.1.1:] It neutralized, because it was furthest away from the syllable that carried stress, which is assumed to be the ultima. All Berawan languages have final syllable stress, so it is most likely that PBn also had that feature.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress in Long Jegan (East) Berawan falls on the final syllable (the ultima) of the word, as in all Berawan lects; words are at most trisyllabic, and the ultima is also the only syllable hosting the full vowel set, vowel-length contrasts, diphthongs/triphthongs and (in its onset) geminate consonants.
new_statements.exceptions: None mentioned; stated as a flat property of the lect. (Sister-lect detail from Clayre & Wan 1996:212 for Long Terawan: final stress realised by length and higher/rising pitch rather than amplitude, same pattern in sentence utterances.)
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level statement in a section on syllable/word phonotactics ('LJG word'), based on elicited lexical items (citation forms); no phrase-level discussion in Burkhardt.
new_statements.identity_note: Burkhardt 2014 treats Long Jegan Berawan (his siglum LJG; = Ethnologue/Glottolog East Berawan zbe/east2486, which Burkhardt relabels geographically 'South-West Berawan') in its own chapter section 5.4; the quoted sentence is specifically about LJG. The only Glottolog-listed description (Clayre & Wan 1996, tagged zbe by Glottolog) actually describes the Long Terawan dialect = West Berawan (west2563), so its p.212 stress statement is a sister-lect statement, not an East Berawan one. Burkhardt gives the same final-stress statement for all four lects (LTN west2563 p.56, BB and LTU = Central Berawan cent2317? [zbc] p.64/§5.3.2, LJG p.77) and for Proto-Berawan (p.193).

sources.note: Ch. 5 synchronic phonologies of all four lects. Long Jegan (LJG = East Berawan) sec. 5.4.2.1 p.77: 'Like the other Berawan languages, LJG has final syllable stress.' Also BB p.64 'The language possesses final syllable stress', LTU sec. 5.3.2 'same syllable stress... as Batu Belah', LTN p.56 'Stress is on the final syllable (Clayre 1996a:212)', PBn p.193 'Since all Berawan languages possess ultimate syllable stress, PBn etyma are reconstructed with ultimate syllable stress.' No discussion of secondary stress or phonetic correlates.

sources.note: Describes LONG TERAWAN dialect (West Berawan, west2563), not Long Jegan. p.212 sec. 2.0: 'The nuclear syllable (S) is the ultimate syllable of the word... Stress in Berawan falls on the nuclear syllable (S). It is marked by length and by higher, often rising, pitch, and not by high average amplitude. The same pattern was also recognized in sentence utterances (see García-Bellido and Clayre 1997 §4.1.3. and Fig. 5b).' Remaining pp. 213-240 not in the preview.
